Chapter Three: Separating Real Preparation from Avoidance.
Let's be honest—sometimes, what feels like “getting ready” is really just a clever way of putting things off. Sure, a little planning and research are important, but there's a fine line between actual preparation and avoidance that looks productive on the surface.
Have you ever caught yourself lost in endless research, or making elaborate plans, just to dodge the uncomfortable part—actually starting? That’s resistance at work, convincing you that you need to be *extra* ready before you begin. But recognizing this trick is key if you really want to move forward.
Real preparation? It's focused, it's purposeful, and it’s all about gathering only what you need for your very next step. Anything beyond that—like exhaustive research, detailed outlines, or brainstorming that never ends—can turn into a sneaky form of procrastination.
Picture an entrepreneur getting ready to launch a new product. Of course, it makes sense to know the market, understand what customers want, and sketch out a basic plan. But spending months fine-tuning every detail, or waiting until every possible risk is addressed? That can stop a business before it even starts.
The same thing happens with creative work. Maybe you’ve seen an artist spend weeks organizing supplies or rearranging the studio, all while not putting a single brush to canvas. Or a writer who keeps perfecting their outline, but never writes that first sentence.
So, how do you avoid falling into the trap of over-preparation? Try adopting a “just enough” mindset when it comes to planning.
First, ask yourself: What’s the minimum I need to get started? Focus only on what’s truly essential for that first step. Then, set a limit on how much time you’ll spend researching. Give yourself a deadline—when the timer goes off, it’s time to move into action.
Embrace a little uncertainty, too. Not everything can be predicted or controlled ahead of time—and that’s okay. Let planning be a springboard, not a shield. The goal is for it to help you get moving, not to keep you standing still.
Now, this doesn't mean you should throw caution to the wind or jump in completely unprepared. It’s about noticing when preparation stops being helpful and starts becoming a form of resistance. The real progress happens when you move quickly from planning into doing, using action as your main learning tool.
Here’s a simple metaphor: think of a pilot getting ready for takeoff. The pre-flight checklist is crucial. But at some point, the plane has to leave the ground. No amount of extra checking will ever teach you as much as actually flying.
So, keep your preparation focused and give yourself a time limit. That way, you’ll have more energy for what really matters—the work itself. And you’ll break out of that endless planning cycle, making real, steady progress toward your goals.
